title: Redwood demo: structured output & function calling (JSON mode)
summary: Quick demo of Redwood structured output (JSON mode) and function/tool-calling. Covered schema enforcement, guardrails, Console integration, and benchmarking considerations. Customer interested in hosted vs dedicated tradeoffs, VPC/KMS, and pilot steps.
next_steps: Alex to share pricing tiers and seat/throughput estimates
Samira to send security pack (SOC 2 + architecture + KMS notes)
Schedule SE-led benchmark with sample prompts (customer to provide schema and 500 sample queries)
Follow-up demo for integrations (ticketing + internal tool calling) week of 2027-12-06
action_items: Alex Moreno - Send pricing + throughput estimate - due 2027-12-03
Samira Patel - Share security & SOC2 docs, KMS integration notes - due 2027-12-02
Priya Rao - Provide sample JSON schema and 500 sample prompts for benchmarking - due 2027-12-04
Jordan Li - Prepare benchmark plan and capacity sizing doc - due 2027-12-06
transcript: 00:00 - Meeting started, quick intros
00:10 - Alex Moreno: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex, AE on Redwood. With me is Samira our SE and Jordan on solutions. How's everyone today?
00:22 - Mark Chen: Doing good thanks. Excited to see the JSON/structured output stuff, we've got a big internal tool integration planned.
00:35 - Priya Rao: Hi, I'm Priya - basically owning the ML side. Our core ask is reliably returning JSON from models and being able to call internal tools (like ticketing) from model outputs.
00:50 - Alex Moreno: Great, that's exactly what we'll demo. Quick qual: are you leaning hosted or private/dedicated? Any compliance constraints?
01:05 - Tom Brooks: Security is critical. We need SOC2, SSO/SAML, audit logs and KMS for key management. Also some data residency concerns for EU traffic.
01:20 - Elena Alvarez: From infra side we want predictable latency; some endpoints are user-facing so 200-400ms tails matter. Also cost is a factor, we run a lot of inference so unit cost matters.

01:40 - Samira Patel: Noted. Redwood supports hosted, dedicated, and private VPC options. For high-throughput with predictable latency teams often pick Dedicated, and we can route EU traffic to EU regions. We'll show batching/quantization knobs in Optimize that help cost/latency tradeoffs.
02:05 - Alex Moreno: We'll demo JSON mode — schema enforcement, guardrails so your app only gets valid JSON, and function/tool calling so the model can emit a structured call to an internal service.
02:20 - Jordan Li: I'll share my screen — starting with the Redwood Console, the structured output tab. Apologies for any lag, network's a bit spotty on my end.
02:35 - [screen share noise]

03:00 - Jordan Li: Here is a sample schema for an incident-ticket payload: {\"title\": \"string\", \"severity\": \"string\", \"metadata\": {}} — apologies transcription: nested braces may appear wrong in transcript export.
03:25 - Priya Rao: Can Redwood validate that schema and reject or correct outputs? We've seen hallucinated fields in raw LLM outputs.

03:40 - Samira Patel: Yes — JSON mode in Redwood enforces the schema at the runtime layer. You can set strict validation: either fail, sanitize, or map. We also show a quick preview in Console where you can test prompts and the engine returns validated JSON or a specific error code.
04:05 - Mark Chen: Does enforcement add latency? Our concern is extra RTTs.

04:18 - Samira Patel: Good Q. Validation is lightweight — it's an additional parse + schema check. In our tests it's usually <10ms overhead for typical payloads. The bigger latency factors are model choice and sequence length. We can also keep validation on the client side if needed.
04:40 - Tom Brooks: What about guardrails — say only certain values allowed for severity? Can we map unknowns to 'unknown' automatically?
04:54 - Jordan Li: Yep — the Console lets you define enum sets and fallback mappings. You can also add a rule to call a function if field missing or inconsistent.

05:10 - Alex Moreno: Let's demo function calling: model returns structured JSON that includes an action like \"create_ticket\" with payload. Redwood can either emit that to you as an event or directly invoke an HTTP webhook / internal function depending on routing policy.
05:32 - [Jordan sets up an example by calling a mock webhook]
06:00 - Jordan Li: I'm sending a sample prompt: \"Summarize the user's report and produce a JSON ticket payload. If severity high, set priority to P0 and call create_ticket.\"
06:20 - [generator typing noises]
06:35 - System: response received — outputting JSON (truncated in transcript).

06:45 - Jordan Li: The Console shows the validated JSON here. It passed validation and invoked the mock webhook. You can see a log entry in the tracing pane — this shows the request/response, tokens, and whether a function call happened.
07:05 - Priya Rao: How do you handle secrets when invoking internal tools? We can't pass service creds to hosted endpoints.

07:15 - Samira Patel: For private deployments you can keep webhook traffic inside the VPC; for Hosted we integrate with customer-managed secrets via KMS and we support ephemeral auth tokens. We never store long-lived plaintext secrets in Redwood. We also support signing requests.
07:40 - Mark Chen: What's the differentiation vs just doing post-processing client-side?

07:48 - Alex Moreno: Good point. Redwood's advantage is unified runtime observability, low-latency execution, and fewer moving parts. Doing it client-side means extra code, and you lose tracing and token-level cost visibility. Also Redwood Optimize provides recommendations for batching/quantization that directly reduce costs without you manually tuning.
08:10 - Elena Alvarez: We have a high QPS endpoint — how do batching and KV cache interact with structured output? Could batching break schema enforcement?

08:25 - Samira Patel: Batching is per-model, per-route and we've designed validation to run on each response post-generation. KV cache is prefix-based; for structured outputs you might want to disable prefix caching for certain routes to avoid stale context. Optimize shows per-route suggestions.

08:50 - Jordan Li: Quick detour — here's an example of function calling for enrichment. The model returns \"call_tool\": \"lookup_customer\", with params {customer_id}. Redwood routes that to a configured integration which returns enriched data and the model can then produce final JSON. This reduces hallucinations since external facts come from your DB.
09:25 - Priya Rao: Nice. We need to ensure audit logs for every function invocation, with request IDs and user context.
09:36 - Samira Patel: That's standard — request tracing and audit logs are available in Console. For Private deployments you can also stream logs to your SIEM.
10:00 - Alex Moreno: Now let's switch to API demo — quick cURL showing JSON mode. Jordan?

10:10 - Jordan Li: curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"model":"redwood-structured-1","mode":"json","schema_id":"incident-v2","prompt":"..."}' — response: {"status":"ok","json":{...}} — again apologies if transcript mangles quotes.
10:40 - Mark Chen: Do you support streaming validated JSON? We stream tokens for UX reasons.

10:52 - Samira Patel: We support streaming with checkpointed validation: the model streams tokens and Redwood performs incremental validation. For production we recommend full validation at the end to ensure strict schema, but streaming helps with perceived latency.
11:15 - Tom Brooks: Encryption at rest — how are tokens and logs protected?
11:23 - Samira Patel: Default at-rest encryption with provider-managed keys, or bring-your-own keys via KMS/HSM. Logs can be encrypted and we support retention policies per customer.
11:40 - Priya Rao: Benchmarks — can Redwood run a pilot to measure 99p latency and token cost for our workload?
11:52 - Alex Moreno: Yes, that's common. We'll do an SE-led benchmark with your sample prompts, measure tail latency, tokens per response, and recommend model/quantization/batching configs.

12:10 - Jordan Li: I'll show Optimize — it scans historical usage and recommends batching, cache, model quantization. Example: for short JSON outputs we recommended 4-bit quantization on certain GPUs dropping cost by ~35% with minimal quality loss in our evals.
12:40 - Elena Alvarez: Any limits on model variants? We use both open models and fine-tuned models.
12:50 - Samira Patel: We host curated open models and support customer-supplied models for Private/Dedicated. You can pin model versions; rollouts support canary splits and automatic fallback.
13:10 - Mark Chen: Can you show an example of a failed validation and the fallback?

13:25 - Jordan Li: Sure — I'll modify the schema to require \"severity\" enum [critical, high, medium, low]. Now I'll send prompt that outputs \"sev\": \"crit\" — Redwood flags a validation error and returns an error code with suggestion. If configured to sanitize, it maps unknown to \"high\" per rule.
13:55 - [pause as Jordan runs the test]
14:10 - Jordan Li: Error logged here: validation_error, rule_id=enum-mapping, suggestion=map 'crit'->'critical' or reject. You can set an automated transformation pipeline in Console.
14:30 - Priya Rao: For auditing we want a copy of original raw model output plus the sanitized JSON. Is that available?
14:40 - Samira Patel: Yes — Console's trace contains both raw tokens and post-processed JSON. You can keep both for X days per retention settings.
15:00 - Mark Chen: Pricing — what are the main levers? token cost, reserved capacity?

15:08 - Alex Moreno: Hosted has per-token pricing; Dedicated is reserved capacity with committed monthly throughput; Private is licensing plus support. Optimize lowers unit cost by suggesting batching and quantization. We'll share a tailored estimate after we see your QPS and average tokens per call.
15:30 - Elena Alvarez: Integration with our ticketing system (internal REST) — we want to avoid sending PII. Can you redact or mask fields before calling tools?

15:45 - Samira Patel: You can define sanitization rules and transformations in the Console pre-invocation. For more control, use Private deployment so network traffic never leaves your VPC and you can run sensitivity filters in-line.

16:05 - Jordan Li: Quick demo of tool calling + chaining: model calls lookup_customer -> enrich -> if score > .8 call create_ticket. The chain is visible in traces, and you can set retry/backoff policies per integration.
16:35 - Tom Brooks: Retries need to be idempotent. Can Redwood add idempotency keys?
16:42 - Samira Patel: Yes, we support idempotency keys and you can pick which field is key-derived on the route config.
17:00 - Priya Rao: We sometimes require deterministic outputs for certain workflows. How do you handle nondeterminism with structured outputs?

17:12 - Alex Moreno: You can enforce deterministic sampling (temperature 0, top_p) and also leverage function calling to reduce nondeterminism by fetching facts externally. For creative tasks you may want higher temp but for tickets you keep low temp.
17:40 - Mark Chen: Any rough timeline for pilot? We want results before board meeting mid-December.

17:50 - Alex Moreno: Totally doable — propose SE benchmark this week, 2-week pilot, decision by mid-December. We'll aim to have benchmark results within 3-5 business days after we receive sample prompts.

18:10 - Jordan Li: One more Console tip — per-route policy lets you set fallback policies: e.g., if your high-quality model is unavailable, fallback to cheaper variant with degraded fields flagged so you can surface warnings to users.
19:00 - [customer small talk, clarifications]
20:00 - Priya Rao: Are there any limitations on streaming function calls? We want early partial enrichments to appear in UI.
20:12 - Samira Patel: We support partial function call streaming; but final schema validation still runs at completion. For UX you can display partials while validation completes.
21:00 - Alex Moreno: Wrapping up demo section — recap and next steps. We'll send pricing, security docs, and request sample prompts + schema. SE will run benchmark and share results.
21:20 - Mark Chen: Sounds good. Please include estimated cost for both hosted and dedicated options for our 2000 qps peak scenario.
21:35 - Alex Moreno: Will do — Alex to follow up with numbers. Any final Qs?
21:50 - Elena Alvarez: No, thanks. Looking forward to benchmark.
22:00 - Meeting ends (call duration ~48 minutes per recording metadata).
